ai_summary: Scottish wind generation is currently delivering an estimated 1.4 GW, which accounts for 13.9% of installed Scottish wind capacity, amidst a wider GB wind output of 2.5 GW. Supported by this renewable output, Scottish carbon intensity has achieved 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide carbon intensity of 225 gCO2/kWh. Despite this abundance of clean power, structural cross-border transmission bottlenecks prevent surplus energy from flowing freely southward. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 849 MWh, turned down through Balancing Mechanism bids at a constraint cost of about £47,969. To bridge the resulting supply deficit and maintain grid stability, thermal generation was dispatched south of the border, resulting in an estimated 161,329 m3 of gas burned elsewhere to replace it and emitting an avoidable 297 tonnes of CO2. Annualising today's figures highlights the recurring financial burden of network constraints, yielding an estimated total yearly cost of £18 million for curtailment. Shared across national consumption, this balancing friction increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £0.06/MWh, demonstrating the dual economic and environmental cost of delayed transmission reinforcement.
